4803.prule: No Tagbu-specific stress statement exists. The only accent statement in the sole grammar of Tagbu is a group-level one for 'these languages, especially of Ndogo', offered as 'suggestions (I shall not call them rules)' and 'a guide for Ndogo': monosyllables unproblematic; polysyllables are mostly compounds whose every component 'must have its own accent duly stressed'; disyllables have either 'an even stress on both syllables' or 'a real accent on the first' (the latter = words with l, r, n in the second syllable, whose vowel is often lost: mbòro = mbòò, kóró = kóó); 'the accent usually lies on the first syllable of dissyllables' (p. 29), so reduplications carry accents on syllables 1 and 3 (exception mbulàmbulà). Remark V extends the remarks by name to Bviri only; Tagbu (Tangbu) is never named in secs. 4-5 (pp. 15-33). The languages are described as tonal with four levels (low, mid, high, very high, p. 17). No fixed, syllable-count-computable, quantity-insensitive stress position is stated for Tagbu or for the group.
4803.srule: Not described as such: Santandrea 1961 has no secondary-stress notion (sec. 4 'Accent' p. 15-16 and sec. 5 'Tone' pp. 16-33; no 'secondary' token on pp. 13-33). 4805.prule: No word-stress rule is stated by any source. Marsh 1959 describes a two-level word tone system (low vs. high): each word carries one tone level, borne by its 'full' syllables; reduced ('atonal') syllables occur mostly before the tone-bearing part, and once the level is set it continues to the end of the word; word-final atonal syllables are always affixes. The 1958 phoneme sheet marks high 'intonation' with an acute (Li's system); the 1994 practical orthography marks low tone with a grave accent. Stress is mentioned only for Shuswap, by contrast.

4805.tone: Marsh 1959: two tone levels (low, high) plus 'atonal' syllables; one tone level per word on the 'full' syllables, set at the first full syllable and persisting to the end of the word; atonal syllables mostly precede the tone and word-final atonal syllables are affixes; hedged throughout ('I have the impression'). Phoneme sheet (1958): acute = high intonation, unmarked = low (Li's system), 'my record is doubtless inaccurate'; vowel length possibly suprasegmental. Tagish Literacy Workshop 1994: 5-6: practical orthography marks low tone with a grave accent (as in Southern Tutchone), i.e. a low-marked system; Wikipedia's alphabet-chart summary says high tone is marked, so the marking convention differs between sources. No source mentions stress or accent placement for Tagish; 'stress' occurs only in Marsh's contrast with Shuswap.

4806.tone: Source-level: tone, not stress. evidence_works.detail: Field data gathered by the author at the White Tai refugee village of Tung Nghia (Lai Chau dialect) from April 1960 to October 1961 under SIL auspices, principal informant Mrs. Dieu Nang Zane (p. 2 and n. 2); stress observations come from her tapes. Sec. 1.5 'Emphatic stress' (p. 36): 'A slight lengthening of the syllable utterance final is normal. Emphatic stress consists of extra loudness and of lengthening of the vowel and the final sonorant, if there is one; it occurs on syllables utterance finally or medially. On the mid-low and mid tones the pitch may be slightly higher than normally.'... 'The preceding remarks are based on very limited occurrences of the phenomena in my tapes. Further study will be required to confirm the observations made thus far and to make possible a detailed description of stress, intonation, and juncture.' Sec. 1.1 (p. 5): 'The syllable structure in White Tai is identical with its morpheme structure. Only six two-syllable items have been observed in which neither syllable could be identified as a morpheme.' Sec. 1.41 (p. 25) notes that emphatic stress affects some tone allophones. The work describes only emphatic (utterance-level) prominence and utterance-final lengthening on a tone language with monosyllabic morphemes; it gives no word-level stress placement rule and does not conflict with Gedney 1989 [1964].

4813.heavy: 'groupe lourd... c'est-à-dire V̄C ou VCC': a long vowel followed by a consonant, or a short vowel followed by two consonants. Stated as a segmental sequence, not a syllable type: the long vowel plus the following onset counts (dafā́tər, lā́bisah), as does a closed syllable plus the following onset (baqárti, tegámmaʿū); word-final CVC (rúkab) and word-final CV̄ (kátabū) are not heavy; word-final CV̄C (buṭū́n, lābᵊsā́t) is heavy.
4813.dflt: first syllable of the word: rúkab 'knees', kátabū 'they wrote', báqarah 'a cow'
4813.prule: Stress falls on the rightmost heavy sequence in the word, where heavy = V̄C (long vowel followed by a consonant) or VCC (short vowel followed by two consonants), counting from the end of the word; if the word contains no such sequence, stress falls on the first syllable. A word-final CVC (rúkab) or word-final long vowel (kátabū) does not count as heavy.

It was noted in §1.3 that affixes combine with roots to make up phonological words. There are, however, two classes of morpheme which are attached to words in the sense that they are themselves never stressed, yet they do not participate in the word for the purpose of stress …
4818.dloc: §1.3 'Stress and syllabification', p. 218 (archive.org p. 235); secondary stress pp. 218-220; formative/clitic exclusion §1.4 p. 221; optional (a) p. 222
4818.heavy: Not rime weight: the attracting property is vowel height/sonority. 'it occurs on an earlier syllable if that syllable's vowel is lower than the vowel(s) of any succeeding syllables' (a lowest, e/o mid, i/u high; the vowel system is i e a o u). CVC and /a/ syllables attract only secondary stress in part A.
4818.dflt: final syllable of the word (root + affixes), e.g. [ta'man], [u'sol], [ifu'no], [tigi'o], [ˌwa.ˌna.'nan]
4818.prule: Primary stress is fully predictable ('redundant'): by default it falls on the final syllable of the phonological word (root plus affixes, clitics and the formative -a- excluded), but it falls on an earlier syllable whose vowel is lower (a < e,o < i,u in height) than the vowel(s) of every following syllable. Examples: [ta'man], [u'sol], [ifu'no], [tigi'o] (final); ['nanun], ['ŋasol], ['ayan], ['mra.mor]/[mu.'ra.mor], [ka.'na.o.ˌrig], [ku.ˌma.ti.'a.o] (non-final). Non-lexical inserted [i]/[u] in the pre-tonic part A do not attract stress. The source does not say which syllable wins if more than one earlier syllable is lower than everything after it (no example decides it).
4818.srule: Before the primary stress ('part A'): with two or more syllables preceding the primary, secondary stress falls on any (C)VC syllable or any syllable with /a/, otherwise on every second syllable to the left of the primary ([ˌi.fu.'no], [ˌtuf.'no], [ku.ˌma.ti.'a.o], [ˌta.'man]); clashes created by /a/ syllables are optionally removed in words of three or more syllables (/a/ -> [ə]), and in runs of three or more /a/ syllables one unpredictably loses its stress and vowel ([ˌwa.ˌna.'nan] ~ [ˌwan.'nan]). After the primary ('part B'): if two or three syllables follow, a secondary stress falls on the second syllable after the primary regardless of its vowel ([ka.'na.o.ˌrig]), 'often hardly perceptible'.
4818.quote: Primary stress placement in Takia is unusual in that it is related to vowel height. Within a word (which includes affixes but not clitics), primary stress falls by default on the final syllable: tama-n [ta'man] father-3SG 'her/his father'; u-sol [u'sol] 2SG-flee 'you fled'; i-fn-o [ifu'no] 3SG-hit-2SG 's/he hit you'; t-gi-o [tigi'o] 1INC:PL-call-2SG 'we called you'. 4819.dq: primary word stress normally falls on the penultimate vowel and secondary stress on the one or more preceding vowels. By contrast, utterance stress creates a succession of alternated stressed and unstressed vowels.
4819.dloc: Chapter 2 'Brief grammatical sketch', section 2.1 Phonology, p. 7 (p. 18 of the ANU file); stress-marked forms pp. 7-8; question intonation section 2.2.9(b), p. 23.
4819.heavy: Long vowel: 'a long vowel counts as two mora' (p. 7); the stress-marked minimal pairs show a final long vowel taking primary stress (ˈtaku 'my' vs taˈku: 'adze', ˈmano vs maˈno: 'shark', aˈro:ha vs aroˈha:). Geminate consonants are phonemic but are not said to affect stress.
4819.prule: Primary stress on the penultimate 'vowel' where a long vowel counts as two (i.e. the penultimate mora): a word-final long vowel takes primary stress (taˈku: 'adze', maˈno: 'shark', aroˈha: 'underside of chin', feˈtu: 'star', noˈno: 'noddy'), otherwise the penultimate syllable (ˈtaku 'my', ˈmano, aˈro:ha, suruˈmaki, taˈhito, kereˈkere, ha:ˈnota, laˈrana; a non-final long vowel does not attract stress). Right-edge, quantity-sensitive Polynesian pattern; hedged by 'normally'.
4819.srule: Stated to exist, placement not specified: 'secondary stress on the one or more preceding vowels' (i.e. on the vowel or vowels before the primary-stressed penultimate vowel); the source does not say which of several preceding vowels bears it, states no word-level alternation, and marks no secondary stress in any cited form.

4820.prule: No stress rule is stated in any reachable source. Transcription-only evidence: L-Thongkum's first-hand broad-phonetic Tariang forms carry the IPA stress mark before the final (main) syllable in every sesquisyllable (PL-530 Table 9, c. 20 forms; MKS 27 Table 4, nine forms), and her proto-template '*CV(C) ˈ CV(C) is retained in Tariang' (PL-530 p.105, a sound-change statement about cognate words) places the mark before the second syllable. This is consistent with fixed final (main-syllable) stress in iambic sesquisyllables, the usual Bahnaric pattern, but neither paper has a phonology section or any sentence describing stress; the mark is the standard Mon-Khmer minor+main syllable notation (Diffloth's Tarieng column in the same MKS 27 Table 4 writes the same words with schwa presyllables and no stress mark, e.g. pədam / baˈdam 'five', kəcen / kaˈtɕen 'nine'). No word longer than minor+main syllable is attested.
4820.srule: Not mentioned in L-Thongkum 2002 (PL-530: 95-108, whole paper read; no phonology or stress section) nor in L-Thongkum 1997 (MKS 27: 109-117); all cited Tariang forms are monosyllables or one minor + one stressed main syllable, so no word long enough to bear a secondary stress is attested.

4828.dq: The intonation pattern of Tanaina does include a simple form of word-stress, however. [...] There are no phonemic (other than syntactic) stresses or pitches.
4828.dloc: Typescript p. 10 (handwritten '10' top right), section 6 of 41; duplicate carbon copy at p. 38.
4828.heavy: None; Krauss states the penult rule holds 'regardless of morphological structure or vowel-grade', i.e. full vs reduced vowel is explicitly denied as a condition (examples k'ézhezh, tatghéshdneh carry stress on reduced e).
4828.prule: Word stress on the penultimate syllable, regardless of morphological structure or vowel grade (full vs reduced vowel); in verbs the stem is word-final, so the penult is the pre-stem syllable. No tone; stress is not phonemic (only 'syntactic' stress/pitch beyond it).
4828.srule: Not mentioned in Krauss 1973, section 6 (typescript p. 10, the complete stress section): one penult stress per cited word is marked and no secondary, rhythmic or alternating stress is described.
4828.quote: There is no distinctive tone of any kind in Tanaina. (This is also true of Eyak, Ahtena, Upper Kuskokwim, Hupa, and many other Athapaskan languages, especially those which have retained stem-final glottalization where that was present in PA.) The intonation pattern of Tanaina does include a simple form of word-stress, however. The general rule is stress on the penult, regardless of morphological structure or vowel-grade: łnazéldaq 'I'm asleep', łnazíldaq 'you're asleep', k'ézhezh 'he's drinking (tea)', k'ezhézhen 'he who is drinking (tea)', k'ełch'ézhi 'blowfly', nuytelqúxch'q'u 'every day', …

secx.primary_revised_quote: The Dena'ina alphabet does not mark stress, There are differences in the way Dena'inas accentuate their words. The Upper Inlet people always stress the stem syllable, but in Outer Inlet and Inland full vowels (a, i, u) before the stem (or before the final syllable) are stressed.
